outcomes.text: Pose research questions, propose hypotheses and predict outcomes.
Design an investigation with its procedure, data needs, risk assessment and ethics.
Carry out safe, careful investigations using map and field location, and rock and soil sampling and identification.
Present and analyse data for trends, describe error and uncertainty, and justify conclusions with evidence.
Interpret scientific and media texts, judge claims by evidence quality and build arguments.
Use maps, cross sections, stratigraphy and isotopic half-life data to describe spatial relationships and infer ages of rocks and fossils.
Communicate to chosen audiences and purposes, including field data compilations and research reports.
Explain why science depends on clear communication, international conventions, peer review and reproducibility.
Explain that complex models and theories need evidence from many people and disciplines.
Show how advances in one science field influence other sciences, technology and engineering.
Explain how social, economic, cultural and ethical factors shape the use of scientific knowledge.
Describe the beneficial, harmful and unintended consequences of using scientific knowledge.
Explain how scientific knowledge supports valid explanations and reliable predictions.
Use scientific knowledge to evaluate projected impacts and design action for sustainability.
Use present-day processes to infer past events through uniformitarianism.
Build a relative time scale using superposition, cross cutting, inclusions and correlation.
Use radioisotope decay to assign absolute dates and place Earth's age at 4.5 billion years.
Describe Earth's layered interior and the seismic and meteorite evidence for it.
Explain how rocks form from mineral assemblages through the igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock cycle.
Explain soil formation and composition as an interaction of atmosphere, rocks, water and life.

topics.title: Development of the atmosphere and hydrosphere

outcomes.text: Explain how the atmosphere came from volcanic outgassing and was changed by photosynthesising organisms.
Describe the temperature-based layers of the modern atmosphere.
Explain where Earth's surface water came from and its three phases.
Explain how water's special properties make it important to Earth system processes.
Use fossil evidence to date the first life at about 4 billion years ago.
Describe laboratory evidence for life emerging in shallow water or at hydrothermal vents without oxygen.
Explain how interacting spheres give each location unique, dynamic communities.
Infer past environments and communities from sedimentary rocks and fossils.
Use the fossil record to infer diversification of life and ecosystem collapse.

units.title: Unit 2: Earth processes - energy transfers and transformations

outcomes.text: Pose research questions, propose hypotheses and predict outcomes.
Design an investigation with its procedure, data needs, risk assessment and ethics.
Carry out safe, careful investigations using map and field location and environmental sampling.
Present and analyse data for trends, describe error and uncertainty, and justify conclusions with evidence.
Interpret scientific and media texts, judge claims by evidence quality and build arguments.
Use maps, spatial representations, diagrams and flow charts to explain ideas, solve problems and predict.
Communicate to chosen audiences and purposes, including field data compilations and research reports.
Explain why science depends on clear communication, international conventions, peer review and reproducibility.
Explain that complex models and theories need evidence from many people and disciplines.
Show how advances in one science field influence other sciences, technology and engineering.
Explain how social, economic, cultural and ethical factors shape the use of scientific knowledge.
Describe the beneficial, harmful and unintended consequences of using scientific knowledge.
Explain how scientific knowledge supports valid explanations and reliable predictions.
Use scientific knowledge to evaluate projected impacts and design action for sustainability.
Explain that energy is conserved and changes form and moves between objects.
Identify the Sun and Earth's interior as the energy sources for Earth processes.
Explain how solar heat and light drive evaporation and photosynthesis.
Explain how heat and gravity in Earth's interior move tectonic plates through convection, plumes and slab sinking.

topics.title: Energy for atmospheric and hydrologic processes

outcomes.text: Explain how the atmosphere, ozone and surface albedo affect solar energy reaching the surface.
Explain the greenhouse effect.
Explain how air mass movement creates atmospheric circulation that spreads heat.
Explain ocean currents and the global ocean conveyor model.
Explain how atmosphere-ocean interaction can cause anomalies like El Nino and La Nina.
Explain photosynthesis as the main energy transformation and define net primary production.
Explain how energy and matter availability set ecosystem carrying capacity.
Explain how nitrogen and phosphorus cycling involves energy transfer between Earth systems.
Explain how energy is stored short term in organisms and long term in hydrocarbons, coal and kerogens in the carbon cycle.

outcomes.text: Pose research questions, propose hypotheses and predict outcomes.
Design an investigation with its procedure, data needs, risk assessment and ethics.
Carry out safe, careful investigations using spatial analysis, map and field location and environmental sampling.
Present and analyse data for trends, describe error and uncertainty, and justify conclusions with evidence.
Interpret scientific and media texts, judge claims by evidence quality and build arguments.
Use maps and spatial representations to explain ideas, solve problems and predict.
Communicate to chosen audiences and purposes, including field data compilations and research reports.
Explain how ICT and other technologies have enlarged and sharpened the data scientists use.
Explain how models and theories are contested, refined or replaced by new evidence or greater explanatory power.
Explain how social, economic and cultural context affects acceptance of scientific knowledge.
Use scientific knowledge to monitor, assess and evaluate risk.
Explain why science may fail to give definitive answers in public debate because data are lacking or open to question.
Explain why large-scale or Asia-Pacific science often needs international collaboration.
Use scientific knowledge to evaluate projected impacts and design action for sustainability.
Explain why non-renewable resources form over geological time and are not quickly replenished.
Relate the location of fossil fuels, iron ore and gold to their geological setting.
Describe remote sensing and direct sampling used to find and size a deposit.
Explain how resource type, volume and location determine extraction methods.
Explain how extraction affects ecosystems, including hydrologic systems.
Define renewable resources and services replenished over years to decades.
Describe provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural ecosystem services.
Explain how abundance and replenishment rate set sustainable use.
Explain how technology efficiency limits cost-effective renewable energy.
Explain how human activities and natural processes change fresh water availability and quality.
Explain how human activities can push populations below viability and harm ecosystem services.
Explain overharvesting and maximum sustainable yield.
Use the ecological footprint to measure demand from producing, using and disposing of resources.

topics.title: The cause and impact of Earth hazards

outcomes.text: Explain that Earth hazards come from interacting Earth systems and can be mitigated, not prevented.
Explain how plate tectonics causes earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis and how they affect other processes.
Use monitoring data to map hazard zones and predict where and how likely repeat events are.
Explain how major weather systems produce cyclones, floods and droughts and affect other processes.
Explain how human activities such as land clearing change the frequency and intensity of hazards.
Explain how a hazard's impact depends on its location, size and the Earth materials involved.

topics.title: The cause and impact of global climate change

subtopics.title: Causes and effects of climate change

outcomes.text: Describe natural and human causes of climate change over different time scales.
Explain how land clearing and fossil fuel use change atmospheric composition and climate.
Describe climate change effects on species, crops, sea level, rainfall, temperature and ice.

subtopics.title: Evidence and models of climate change

outcomes.text: Use geological, prehistorical and historical records to show regional climate change effects.
Explain how climate models of oceans and atmosphere are built from past and present data to predict change.
